intro: In English, adjectives never change and go before the noun: “a red car”, “red cars”. When you use several adjectives, they follow an order (opinion, size, age, colour, origin, material). This lesson helps you avoid the most common mistakes.
objectifs: Put the adjective before the noun or after a verb like be, look, feel.
Use adjectives with no plural and no female form.
Put several adjectives in the right order (a beautiful old wooden table).
Use a noun like an adjective (a coffee cup, a bus stop).

sections.titre: Before the noun or after the verb
texte: An adjective goes before the noun: “a big house”, “an interesting book”. Never after the noun: “a red car”, not “a car red”.
It can also go after some verbs: be, look, feel, seem, get / become, taste, smell: “The house is big.”, “You look tired.”, “This soup tastes good.”
“A” or “an” depends on the sound of the next word, so often on the adjective: “a car” but “an old car”; “an apple” but “a big apple”.
exemples: We live in a small flat.
The flat is small but comfortable.

texte: English adjectives have no plural and no female form: “a tall man, a tall woman, tall people.”
You can't use an adjective alone as a noun for one person or thing: add “one”, “man”, “woman”, “person”: “the new one”, “a rich man”. (“The rich” exists, but for a whole group.)
exemples: Which dress do you want? — The blue one.

texte: When there are several adjectives before a noun, English follows a fairly fixed order. Opinion (what you think) comes first, then facts: size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, and finally purpose, just before the noun.
In practice, we rarely use more than two or three adjectives. Remember: opinion → size → age → colour → origin → material.
Join two colours with “and”: “a black and white cat”.
exemples: She's got a beautiful old wooden table.
We often eat in a lovely small Italian restaurant.
sections.note: To remember: OSASCOMP (Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Colour, Origin, Material, Purpose).

sections.titre: Adjectives that go only after the verb
texte: Some adjectives that start with “a-” go only after the verb: afraid, alone, asleep, awake, alive. Say “The baby is asleep”, not “an asleep baby”: say “a sleeping baby”.
In British English, “ill” is also used mostly after the verb: “She's ill.” Before a noun, say “a sick child”.
exemples: Don't make noise, the baby is asleep.
I'm afraid of dogs. — He's a frightened child.
afraid after the verb; frightened before the noun.

sections.titre: A noun used like an adjective
texte: English often puts a noun before another noun to describe it. The first noun works like an adjective and stays singular: “a shoe shop”, “a bus stop”, “a coffee cup”.
The main word is the last one: “a coffee cup” is a cup; “a cup of coffee” is the coffee in the cup.
These groups can take an adjective too: “a new shoe shop”, “a big football match”.
exemples: There's a bus stop in front of the school.
My sister works in a shoe shop.
Let's watch the football match tonight.

formule: (a / an) + opinion + size + age + shape + colour + origin + material + NOUN · be / look / feel + adjective
prononciation: In adjective + noun, the main stress is on the noun: “a big HOUSE”, “a red CAR”.
In noun + noun, the stress is on the first noun: “a COFFEE cup”, “a BUS stop”, “a SHOE shop”.
“an” links to the next word: “an old car” = /ən ˈəʊld kɑː/ ≈ “a-nold car”.
“interesting” has three syllables: /ˈɪntrəstɪŋ/ (“in-tres-ting”), stress at the start.
erreurs: The adjective goes before the noun.
Adjective before the noun, no s; “people” is the plural of “person”.
A noun used like an adjective stays singular.
She is a woman very nice.
Very + adjective goes before the noun.

dialogue.contexte: At Brussels airport, Moana can't find her bag. She describes it to the man at the lost property office.
lignes: Good morning. How can I help you?
I can't find my bag. I think it's on the plane from Montreal.
OK. What does it look like?
It's a small black leather bag.
Is it a backpack or a handbag?
A handbag. It's got a long thin strap and a little silver key ring.
Let me check… Is this your bag?
No, that's a big brown bag. Mine is black.
Yes! That's it! Thank you so much!
“That's it” = that is the right one.

exercices.consigne: Add the adjective in brackets in the right place.
items: She lives in a big house.

exercices.consigne: Put the adjectives in the right order before the noun.
Each phrase or sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: Look, a sleeping baby. / Look, the baby is asleep.

exercices.consigne: Describe three things you like (a piece of clothing, a piece of furniture, a personal thing). Use at least two adjectives for each, in the right order.
items: I love my old blue jeans. In my living room there's a big round wooden table. And I always carry a small black leather wallet.

a_retenir: Adjective before the noun (a red car) or after be / look / feel / seem (The car is red).
Adjectives never change: no s, no female form (red cars, a tall woman).
Order: opinion – size – age – shape – colour – origin – material – noun (a beautiful old wooden table).
afraid, alone, asleep, awake, alive: only after the verb.
Noun + noun: the first noun stays singular (a shoe shop, a bus stop).
